newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Olympics no bonanza, Sydney businesses told.
newsitem.headline: Olympics no bonanza, Sydney businesses told.

text.p: Sydney business leaders were told on Wednesday not to expect too big an economic spinoff from the city's hosting of the 2000 Olympic Games.

Presenting what it said was the first official report card on the economic impact of the recent Atlanta Games, the New South Wales (NSW) Chamber of Commerce said businesses should be realistic in their expectations.
The chamber was backed up by NSW state premier Bob Carr, who told reporters: "It would be foolish to say the Olympic Games are an economic bonanza."
Citing figures from the Georgia State University Economic Forecasting Centre, the chamber said that the Olympics generated US$4 billion for the Georgia economy.
That figure was below pre-Games estimates of around $5.1 billion -- and a top-range estimate by one Atlanta organiser of a $10 billion contribution to the Georgian economy.
Although Georgia's economic growth this year, at around 5.0 percent, would be well above the U.S. national average, it would still lag the 5.1 percent achieved in 1995.
Chamber chief executive Katie Lahey said that Atlanta's growth rate rose sharply in the run-up to the Games, but was now declining just as sharply.
Almost 100,000 jobs were generated during May and June but very few were long-term and unemployment was forecast at 4.9 percent next year, rising to 5.6 percent in 1998.
"These economic indicators are vitally important for Sydney's planning and forecasting of the potential benefits," Lahey said in a statement.
"There was a lot of good news out of the Games, but some disappointment. It highlights the need to be realistic in our expectations."

Lahey cited the example of hotel occupancy -- original forecasts for the Games predicted that only 35 percent of visitors would stay with friends and relatives, but the final figure was closer to 70 percent, she said.

One positive fact thrown up by the Atlanta research was that locals were able to but tickets more easily than expected. A lot of Sydney residents fear they will not be able to compete with tourists and corporate guests in the 2000 ticket rush.
Lahey said Sydney had to carry on monitoring the cost and benefits for Atlanta to ensure that its own businesses could plan for the Games.

At a luncheon speech outlining his expectations for the Games, Carr said a sharp rise in television rights revenues -- more than $1.1 billion is guaranteed -- and sponsorship deals already ruled out the New South Wales government having to pick up any losses for the Games.
